chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Jundab, who said:

I asked Abu Al-Hasan Al-Mazi (peace be upon him be peace (about) what I should say in the prostration of gratitude, for our companions differed regarding it, so he (peace be upon him) said: Say while you are prostrating.

O Allah, I bear witness to You, and I bear witness to Your angels, and Your prophets, and Your messengers, and all of Your creation, that You are Allah my Lord, and Islam is my religion, and Muhammad is my prophet, and Ali, and so-and-so, and so-and-so, up to the last of them, are my Imams. With them I befriend and from their enemies I disavow.

O Allah, I adjure You by the blood of the oppressed (three times). O Allah, I adjure You by Your promise upon Yourself regarding Your guardians, that You make them victorious over Your enemy and their enemy, that You send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the protected ones from the family of Muhammad. O Allah, I ask You for ease after difficulty (three times).

Then place your right cheek on the ground and say: O my refuge, when the paths weary me and the earth is straitened for me despite its vastness, and O Creator of my creation, have mercy on me, although You were needless of my creation. Send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the protected ones from the family of Muhammad.
Then place your left cheek (on the ground) and say: O Humiliator of every tyrant, and O Honorer of every humbled one. And I swear by Your Might that my striving has reached its end (three times).
Then say: O Affectionate, O Bestower, O Remover of great distress (three times).
Then return to prostration and say one hundred times: Thank You, Thank You. Then ask for your need, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.
ai.seo_question: What are the specific words and actions for the prostration of gratitude in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Kafi, this hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) prescribes a comprehensive supplication for Sajdat al-Shukr that integrates theological affirmation with political loyalty to the Imams. It uniquely emphasizes the concept of 'anshodu' (adjuring) by the blood of the oppressed, reflecting the Shia tradition of connecting gratitude to divine justice and the eventual triumph of the Ahl al-Bayt. The ritual concludes with repeated expressions of thanks, highlighting the spiritual discipline of maintaining gratitude even amidst worldly trials.
